At the same time, we find examples that differ sharply or directly contradict one another.

This leads us to conclude that the similarities, differences, and contradictions between these forms of knowledge come from social rather than merely individual starting points, and from objective rather than merely subjective conditions.
This conclusion brings us closer to the root of the issue.
Here again, we can turn to the different forms of knowledge that have been produced, from various periods down to the present, about the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage.
Examining these forms is one of the main tasks of this introduction, although we have not yet reached the proper place for that discussion.
Nothing prevents us, however, from anticipating its results here and using them as part of our search for a scientific solution to the relationship between the Arab present and the heritage.
We will find that behind every form of “knowledge” about this heritage produced by a historian, interpreter, or researcher, ancient or modern, there is an ideological position.
At its root, an ideological position is a class position.
This class position does not have to appear openly in every individual case. It may instead be hidden within the intellectual foundation from which a particular interpretation of the heritage begins.
This is not something unique to the Arab-Islamic heritage.
It is a rule, or something close to a general law, that applies here just as it applies to every attempt to understand any part of humanity’s heritage in any period of civilization.
We can begin with an example close to us.
Among contemporary Arab writers who study the history of philosophy, we find different attempts to understand the ancient Greek philosophical heritage.
When they try to identify the main philosophical direction of a great Greek thinker such as Aristotle, two major and very different forms of interpretation appear.

One tries with great effort to bring out the idealist sides of Aristotle’s teachings and hide their materialist sides. At times, it even distorts or misrepresents those sides in order to turn the basic direction of Aristotle’s philosophy away from its materialist tendency and toward pure idealism.
Against this, we find another kind of interpretation.
It concentrates on the materialist tendencies in Aristotelian philosophy without ignoring the idealist weaknesses that are also present in it.
Nor does it overlook the lack of consistency within Aristotle’s philosophical system.
On the one hand, Aristotle deals with the problem of matter and form in an idealist way. On the other, he puts forward the materialist principle that being exists prior to consciousness.
We understand the difference between these two ways of reading the same philosophical heritage of the same philosopher as a difference in intellectual and ideological starting point.
This becomes even clearer when we remember the relationship between Aristotle’s heritage and the heritage of Arab-Islamic philosophy.
Arab-Islamic philosophy built its relationship with Aristotle on the basis of central principles in his thought.

Historically, those principles opened a path toward questioning the carefully organized idealist structure Plato had built in opposition to the seeds of philosophical materialism planted before him by thinkers such as Thales, Anaximander, and Democrates among the Ionian philosophers, and by Democritus, one of the founders of atomism.

A particular intellectual and ideological starting point lies behind the concentrated attacks on the relationship between Aristotle’s logical and philosophical heritage and the heritage of the leading Muslim logicians and philosophers of the medieval Arab-Islamic world.

The same starting point lies behind the completely dismissive view that some revivalists, both old and modern, have taken toward that relationship—a view that conflicts with both historical and scientific reasoning.
In this total rejection, we can detect hostility toward some of the materialist sides of Aristotle’s philosophy.
This is especially clear in the distinctly materialist character of his criticism of Plato’s theory of Forms, and in the even clearer materialist basis of his theory of knowledge.

It is useful here to make a brief side observation about the sharply different, and sometimes completely opposite, positions taken toward Aristotle’s heritage in Europe during the Middle Ages and at the beginning of the Renaissance.
These differences appeared among intellectual and philosophical schools that were subject to Christian theological authority, especially those that held powerful positions within the universities.
Anyone familiar with the history of this period knows how attitudes toward Aristotle’s philosophy moved between two extremes.
At one point, studying Aristotle could be forbidden, with severe punishments imposed on anyone who “committed” the offense.
At another, the study of Aristotle could itself become compulsory, with equally severe punishments imposed on anyone who “committed” the offense of refusing it.
What explains such different and contradictory positions toward the philosophical heritage of one and the same philosopher?
The reason was that “knowledge” of that heritage took on the character of the intellectual and ideological foundation that governed how this knowledge was produced.
To confirm this point, we can look at another striking fact familiar to anyone who follows the history of philosophy: the many different ways in which that history has been interpreted.
The history of philosophy is one history.
Why, then, are there so many different ways of explaining it?
There may be more than one reason.
One reason may be the obvious complexity of the history of philosophy itself and the difficulty of fully tracing the many overlapping relationships between causes and events within it.
But from our point of view, the strongest reason is the difference in the indirect aims of historians of philosophy.
We should not treat these aims as purely private or personal.
When the different ways of interpreting the history of philosophy are classified scientifically, their differences fall into broader currents and schools rather than into isolated personal opinions.

This supports the conclusion that ideological starting points are the main reason these different forms of “knowledge” take different directions and use different methods to interpret the history of philosophy.
These differences in direction and method even affect the way historians divide the history of philosophy into periods.
The great majority of historians of philosophy who begin from bourgeois ideologies use different measures when they divide philosophical history into stages.
Very often, these measures are fundamentally unhistorical.

They may divide philosophy simply by centuries, by the dates of royal dynasties, by the rise and disappearance of particular schools, or by the appearance and disappearance of particular ideas, and so on.
By using measures of this kind, they avoid seeing the specific material and historical basis behind changes from one stage of philosophy to another.
To begin from that material and historical basis means recognizing that philosophy appears in developed societies as an indirect and highly developed reflection of material existence.
Because philosophy has this character, its development corresponds, to one degree or another, to the historical development of social existence itself.
This means that when we divide the history of philosophy into stages, we should begin from the same basic measures used to divide the history of human society.
In other words, we begin from the rise and development of different social formations and from the replacement of one by another.
On this basis, the materialist view of history divides the history of philosophy into the following stages:
The philosophy of the transition from feudalism to capitalism.
The philosophy of the age of imperialism and proletarian revolutions, from the late nineteenth century to the October Socialist Revolution in Russia.
The philosophy of the age of building socialism and communism, beginning with the appearance of socialism in one country and its later development into a world system.

Dividing the history of philosophy in this way does not mean that the materialist view of history ignores the separate stages within each social formation, or the smaller stages within each historical period.

For example, it recognizes the different stages in the development of capitalist relations in Europe: the early bourgeois revolutions of the seventeenth century, the preparation for the French Revolution and the revolution itself in the eighteenth century, and the period leading up to the more advanced revolutions of 1848–1849.
It also recognizes that philosophy itself develops through different levels within each of these smaller periods.
This is how we should understand the special place Marxism gives to classical German philosophy.
While always stressing that all historical periodization is relative, Marxism still treats this German philosophical tradition as having a certain degree of independence of its own.

We have gone into some detail about these different ways of dividing the history of philosophy into stages, and about the different intellectual and methodological assumptions behind them, for one reason: to stress that differences of this kind ultimately rest on ideological differences—that is, on an implicit form of class “partisanship.”

This partisanship appears in interpretations of the history of philosophy just as it appears in philosophy itself. At every stage in the development of society—whether in Europe, the Arab-Islamic world, India, or China—philosophy developed through the struggle between materialism and idealism. The history of philosophy is interpreted through the same struggle.

Whether bourgeois philosophers and historians admit it or not, they too begin from partisan positions: from the standpoint of the interests of one class or social group rather than another. Materialists, for their part, must not respond by ignoring idealist thinkers or simply dismissing them. A materialist must treat idealists and their philosophies, first, as historical realities that need to be understood, and second, as ideas that must be subjected to constructive criticism.
This was precisely the attitude Marx and Engels took toward Hegel, and it reflects the partisan character of philosophy.

The partisanship of idealist histories of philosophy usually appears in a different form. Idealist historians often avoid an open confrontation with materialism altogether. They ignore materialist thinkers, or they try to distort the materialist content of their philosophy.

The same thing happened to the materialist elements of Arab-Islamic philosophy, and to ancient Indian and Chinese philosophy. Idealism tried to exclude materialism from philosophy by relying on a simple formula: materialism is hostile to religion; philosophy and religion are one; therefore materialism does not belong to philosophy and should not be treated as one of its subjects.

This position is itself one form of the partisanship of idealist philosophy, even though idealist philosophers deny that philosophy is partisan at all and refuse to recognize its division into materialism and idealism. They therefore classify philosophy according to standards that appear “non-partisan”—in other words, free of class interests—and divide it instead into different schools.

When materialism insists that idealism cannot simply be ignored, it is also recognizing the role of historical necessity. Idealism arose under particular historical conditions because those conditions made its appearance necessary.

Behind this position lies a basic principle of historical materialism: the way a society produces its material goods plays the decisive role in the rise and development of social ideas, including philosophical ideas. Class struggle, in turn, inevitably affects the development of ideology, philosophy included.

Everything we have said so far about understanding the intellectual heritage points to an important fact. The method we use to understand that heritage, and the scientific tools we bring to it, are shaped less by the heritage itself and the social conditions of its own age than by the time in which our new understanding is produced and by the social position of the people producing it.
As we have already seen, these present-day conditions form the ideological basis of the particular way in which the heritage is understood.

This means that every view of the heritage contains, within it, a view of the past from the standpoint of the present—whatever historical period that “present” happens to be. Our understanding of the heritage is therefore a product of the present, not a product of the past in which the heritage itself was created.
This applies to every way of looking at the heritage, whatever ideological form that understanding takes.
Even the rigid traditionalist outlook that has become so prominent in recent ideological struggles in the Arab world does not escape this rule.

Traditionalists may insist on seeing the present through the past rather than the past through the present. They may try to carry ideas from the past—with all the social meanings they had in an earlier age, meanings that historical development has already left behind—into the present, and put them in place of the new realities created by that development.
But even when they insist on looking at the heritage in this way, they are in fact starting from the opposite direction.

Their real starting point is the place occupied in the present social structure by a particular class whose ideology they express. They may belong directly to that class, or their position may result from other factors connected with their intellectual formation and with the character of their political and class consciousness.

In other words, the real content of their traditionalist view of the heritage—their attempt to impose the past on the present—has its roots in the present itself. It grows out of the soil of the present.

It is one form taken by the ideological conflicts of our own time. It reaches into the “museum” of the past for ideas that have hardened there, and uses them to shore up a class position that is becoming unstable within a social structure being broken apart by the pressures of the present.

The point, then, is that there is no single relationship between the present and the heritage, because the present itself is not one single thing. And because the heritage is viewed from within the present, it too does not appear as one single thing.

The class structure of Arab societies today takes different forms from one society to another. The struggles taking place within them also differ in character. Yet across these different societies, one new reality has become increasingly clear: the growing conflict between different positions on the central questions that now demand answers—the national question, the social question, democracy, and intellectual life.

As these questions have become more closely connected, and as the boundaries between them have almost disappeared, the conflicts around them have grown sharper. The differences between opposing positions have become wider and deeper.
This has made one fact increasingly clear: the meaning of the “present” is not the same for every class and every social group.

Each occupies a different position within the process of change now shaking existing social structures. Each also understands differently where this process is heading and how it is moving. And for each class or group, the direction of that movement may fit—or conflict with—its own ambitions, interests, and future.

The “present” experienced by classes and groups whose positions are weakening and becoming unstable is therefore not the same as the “present” experienced by those whose position is becoming stronger and more deeply rooted in the current Arab liberation movement.
The first has a past-oriented present. The second has a future-oriented present.

The first relates to the past like a drowning person clinging to a piece of wood. The second relates to it as the coming age relates to an earlier age that is being transformed through the movement of the present.

And just as the “present” of one class position differs from the “present” of another, and just as each relates differently to the past, the “heritage” itself also takes a different form for each of them.
The heritage appears within each ideological outlook in the same way that the present appears within it, and in the same way that its relationship with the past is understood.
This is how we discover that the heritage is not, in this sense, one single thing.
It becomes many different heritages because it is viewed from the present, and—as we have seen—the present itself is divided.
What we mean here, of course, is that there are many different ideological and class views of the heritage. As a historical reality, the heritage itself remains one.
The revolutionary forces within the Arab liberation movement therefore have their own future-oriented “present,” distinct from the past-oriented “present” of backward-looking forces.
They also have their own “heritage,” distinct from the heritage seen by those other forces.

What, then, are the main features of this heritage as it appears to revolutionary forces? What kind of understanding allows them to grasp the intellectual heritage of the medieval Arab-Islamic world? And how does the heritage look different from this revolutionary perspective than it does from a backward-looking one?
